comment: Why a SwiftUI symbol is absent from TUIkit, on purpose.
renamed        - the capability exists under a different name. 'tuikit' is that
name, and the tool checks it still exists.
notImplemented - deliberately absent. 'why' must say what a CHARACTER GRID cannot
express, not merely that the API sounds graphical.
differentShape - the capability exists but not as a one-to-one symbol; 'how'
is prose and is NOT machine-checked, so keep it short and true.
families       - glob patterns, for whole families that share one reason.
An entry explains everything inside it: explaining AccessibilityRotor also explains
AccessibilityRotor.Body. Anything neither explained here nor listed in baseline.json
is reported as a gap. Run with --stale to have the tool check these entries back
against both frameworks; an entry that has gone wrong is worse than no entry.

families.why: A terminal has no assistive-technology stack: no VoiceOver, no rotor, no accessibility tree for anything to read. The screen reader IS the terminal's own, driven by the text TUIkit already emits, so contrast and labelling are the levers that carry over — and those are TUIkit's own API.
Xcode canvas metadata. It has no runtime meaning in any app, on any platform.

Multi-contact input. MagnifyGesture and RotateGesture recognize the scale and the angle between two contacts, a trackpad pinch or twist; SpatialEventGesture reports every simultaneous contact as an identified event with a kind (touch, pencil, pinch, pointer), a 3D location and the input device's pose. A terminal's mouse protocols (X10, SGR 1006) report one pointer: its cell, its buttons, the wheel and the Shift/Option/Control bits. There is no second contact, no pinch or twist and no pose, so no scale, angle or contact set to recognize. The single-pointer gestures ship (TapGesture, SpatialTapGesture, LongPressGesture, DragGesture and their algebra), and WindowDragGesture is declined with the Window family.

Sub-cell typography, as the View modifiers of the same names (decisions C8): a cell grid has one advance per cell, one baseline and one line height, so kerning, tracking, a baseline offset or a line height have nowhere to go. A run's paragraph alignment has no carrier either: a Text aligns its lines as one block (multilineTextAlignment), never paragraph by paragraph. Omitted so setting one fails to compile.

An adaptive image glyph (Genmoji) is a multi-resolution bitmap drawn inline at the font's size. A terminal cell holds a character, and the image protocols that can place a picture are block-level, not glyphs in a run of text.

The keys' Codable conformances (macOS 26) need Codable values, and TUIkit's Color (which can name a palette role or carry a gradient) and Font are not Codable. An attributed string with these attributes still compiles and draws; it does not archive them.

macOS 26's rich-text editing: a TextEditor over an AttributedString and the definitions constraining what an edit may set. It waits on an attributed TextEditor, which Text(AttributedString) now makes possible (decisions A42).
Standard-library conformance members. They appear on both sides wherever the type does, so comparing them measures Hashable and Collection, not parity.
Every View has one. Where TUIkit implements the view it has a body too, so a difference here only ever means the TYPE is absent — which is reported on the type itself.

TUIkit has `Animatable`, `AnimatablePair`, `AnimatableValues` and `VectorArithmetic`, and interpolates through them. What stays absent under this rule: the conformances on types TUIkit does not have (CoreGraphics geometry, decisions C1; SwiftUI's shapes, O0 of the refusal review; `Color.ResolvedHDR`, A16), the deprecated `AnimatableModifier`. The `@Animatable`/`@AnimatableIgnored` macros ship in the opt-in `TUIkitMacros` product (decisions A52), which this tool does not extract: macros are not in its symbol graphs.

The typeface axes: naming a family, asking for a point size, scaling one, or widening it. A terminal emulator draws every cell in the one font at the one size its user configured, and no escape sequence asks it for another — so each of these could only be accepted and ignored. TUIkit's Font (Sources/TUIkitFoundation/Styling/Font.swift) carries the axes that DO survive: the semantic style, weight and italic.

Small caps is a glyph variant inside a typeface — real capitals at x-height. A terminal font has one glyph per codepoint and no variant table. `View.textCase(.uppercase)` is not this API under another name: it substitutes different CHARACTERS, changing what the text says and (for ß → SS) how many cells it needs.

SwiftUI can put a searchable field's suggestions in two places — a pop-up menu, or in the content beneath the field — so it needs a placement type and a per-placement visibility. TUIkit has one place: the field's drop-down (Sources/TUIkitTextInput/Views/TextInputSuggestions.swift, the same DropdownMenu the Picker uses). `View.searchSuggestions(_:)` and `View.searchCompletion(_:)` are implemented against it. Shipping the `for:` overload would mean either honouring one case of an OptionSet and silently ignoring the other — the partial-seam shape declined twice in Documentation/Historical/Parity work blocked on a decision (2026-10-12).md — or inventing an in-content suggestions surface, which is a feature rather than parity plumbing.

The `image:` spelling of these initializers names an `ImageResource` — a symbol the Xcode build generates from an asset catalogue, whose value is a raster bitmap at one of several scale factors. A terminal app has neither: no asset catalogue in the build (SwiftPM resources are files, not named image constants), and no way to place a bitmap in a cell. The `systemImage:` spelling of every one of these IS implemented (Sources/TUIkitFoundation/SFSymbols/ControlSymbolInitializers.swift, and PickerSymbolInitializers.swift beside it), because an SF Symbol is a character: it resolves to a Private-Use scalar the terminal font may carry, and falls back to the title alone when it does not. `Label(_:image:)` and `ContentUnavailableView(_:image:description:)` with an image NAME (a String) ship, the name found as `Image(_:bundle:)` finds a resource file (refusal review P12); their `ImageResource` forms share the parity key and stay declined by this rule.

The `formatter:` spelling is the pre-`FormatStyle` class API. It parses through an untyped out-parameter — `Formatter.getObjectValue(_:for:errorDescription:)` yields `AnyObject` — so binding it to a `Binding<Int>` is a downcast the compiler cannot check, and SwiftUI's `Text`/interpolation overloads narrow it further to `NSObject` and `ReferenceConvertible`, which are Objective-C bridging protocols rather than Swift ones. The same capability IS implemented in its typed form, where `Strategy.ParseOutput == FormatInput` makes the round-trip a static guarantee: `TextField(_:value:format:)` and its two siblings (Sources/TUIkitTextInput/Views/TextFieldValue.swift), `Text(_:format:)` (Sources/TUIkitFoundation/Views/Text.swift:111) and `\(value, format:)` in a LocalizedStringKey interpolation. Adding the class spelling beside them would be the same feature with the type safety taken out.

Wrapping an AppKit view, view controller, gesture recogniser or app delegate inside SwiftUI. There is no AppKit on a character grid, and TUIkit must also build on Linux, where none of these types exist. The escape hatch a terminal offers instead is `Renderable` — a view that assembles its own cells — not a bridge to a second view system.

Per-pixel shading: Metal shader functions, colour/layer/distortion effects, blur, blend modes, luminance to alpha, the background extension effect (a mirrored, blurred copy) and dynamic range. Every one of them addresses a sample. A terminal cell has one foreground colour, one background colour and a glyph, with no subpixel to shade. `View.opacity` is the one filter that survives, and it survives by resolving at composite time against whatever is behind it (see Documentation/Colour and styling/Opacity as composition.md) rather than by blending pixels. Glass ships as a material's surface with a highlighted rim, no refraction (refusal review O5, Deliberate deviations C11).
visionOS: three-dimensional spatial events, immersive spaces, world tracking, the compositor and RealityKit content. A terminal is a flat grid of cells with no depth, no head pose and no hands.
Apple Pencil hover, squeeze and double-tap. Hardware a terminal cannot see: its input is bytes arriving on a file descriptor.
The Touch Bar — a strip of pixels on a keyboard Apple no longer ships. No terminal has one to draw into.

Windows on a desktop, managed by its window server: their size, position, placement, level, style and resizing, dragging one by its background, full screen and minimising, the display they are on, which open at launch and which are restored, which handles an external event, and the menu-bar extra. A TUI app's windows share one surface, the terminal it was launched in, as covers stacked over one another (refusal review O9, ruled (b): they open, close and come to the front, which TUIkit does), and that surface's size is the user's terminal emulator's, announced by SIGWINCH: there is nothing for the application to size, place, raise above another app or restore.

The document architecture, the Services menu, and the file panels lane O10 has not reached yet. DocumentGroup and its configurations read and write through FileWrapper, which Linux's Foundation lacks, and ReferenceFileDocument is an ObservableObject, a family TUIkit does not have (compatibility guide §2.3). The Services menu (exportsItemProviders, importsItemProviders, exportableToServices, importableFromServices) is macOS's system-wide menu of other apps' services, which a terminal app has no way into. `fileImporter`, `fileMover` and the `fileDialog` customizations ship: TUIkit draws the open panel in a sheet (TUIkitFilePanels; decisions File panels (O10)).

Writing Tools: Apple's on-device language models, which macOS presents over a text view to proofread, rewrite and summarise. A terminal app has no such service to call. (The in-app find bar this family once also declined ships for TextEditor: findNavigator, findDisabled, replaceDisabled and FindContext, refusal review P17.)

`onCommand(_:perform:)` answers a command sent up the responder chain by an Objective-C `Selector` (a menu item's action, a `NSResponder` message). TUIkit has no responder chain and no Objective-C runtime on Linux; its menu bar's commands (TUIkitCommands) are views with actions, and what reaches the focused view is SwiftUI's own focus-path commands (`onMoveCommand`, `onExitCommand`, `onDeleteCommand`, `onCopyCommand`, `onCutCommand`, `onPasteCommand`). Declined since refusal review O13 (CONFIRM).
WidgetKit configurations and control widgets. They are built by a separate extension process that the system renders into the Home Screen and Control Centre. A terminal app is not one.
ShareLink and its previews present the system share sheet, which enumerates other applications' share extensions. Outside a windowed OS session there is no such registry to enumerate.

The modifiers, environment values and initialisers over Image.Scale, SymbolRenderingMode, SymbolColorRenderingMode and SymbolVariableValueMode, whose types are declined above. An SF Symbol here is one codepoint drawn at the terminal's font size in the cell's single foreground colour (Sources/TUIkitStrings/SFSymbols/SFSymbol.swift). So there is no relative size to pick (macOS honours imageScale: 17×16 → 23×20 points, measured), no layers to colour separately (macOS draws even single-layer `star` differently under .hierarchical), and no variable-value layers to fill. Confirmed in Documentation/SwiftUI parity/Refusals re-examined, wave 17 (2026-10-03).md (Symbols).

Sub-cell typography: kerning and tracking move glyphs by fractions of a point, baselineOffset raises a run within its line, and lineHeight sets the distance between baselines. Cells advance in whole columns and rows, and the emulator places each glyph within its cell, so none of these could be more than accepted and ignored. Confirmed in Documentation/SwiftUI parity/Refusals re-examined, wave 17 (2026-10-03).md (P8's omissions, and the Font.Leading verdict: a grid can only move whole rows).

Affordances the operating system draws over a text view: Apple Intelligence's Writing Tools button, and the rich-text formatting control bar. Nothing in a terminal app is OS-drawn, and neither service reaches a terminal. TextInputFormattingControlPlacement is declined for the same reason (Documentation/SwiftUI parity/Refusals re-examined, wave 17 (2026-10-03).md).

A run's typesetting language sets its line height, line breaking and spacing. Line height is the terminal's row and spacing is whole cells; TUIkit's word wrapper breaks at spaces and at characters a line cannot hold, whatever the language. So a language changes none of the three and could only be accepted and ignored. See Documentation/SwiftUI parity/Decisions/SwiftUI API completion decisions.md C8.
visionOS: immersive spaces, Compositor Services content, hand-gesture shortcuts and world recentring. None of these is available on macOS, and a terminal has no space to be immersed in.

WidgetKit controls and system surfaces: Control Center and Lock Screen controls, a widget's invalidatable content, interaction tracking for system intelligence, and iOS Assistive Access's navigation icon. Each is drawn by the system outside the app, and no such surface reaches a terminal app.

AppKit bridges: SwiftUI content hosted in an NSMenu or an NSWindow sheet, scene representations for NSApplication, AppKit animations driven by a SwiftUI Animation, and conversions to AppKit value types. TUIkit draws no AppKit views, and AppKit is absent on Linux and Windows; Renderable is the escape hatch for drawing of an app's own.

Handoff and URL delivery: NSUserActivity continuation, and URLs opened from elsewhere arriving at the app. Both come through the app's bundle registration with LaunchServices, which a command-line program run in a terminal has none of; nothing can send it a URL or an activity.

iOS device and lifecycle features: interface orientation (for previews and supported orientations), background tasks woken by the system, and the home indicator and other persistent system overlays. A terminal app has none of them, on any platform.

Core Data, which exists only on Apple's platforms. Permitted, not declined: under decisions A18 (owner, 2026-10-12, option 1) Apple-only API is allowed behind #if canImport where it is honoured on Apple platforms, so the family would compile and work for an Apple-only app and be absent on Linux and Windows, where Core Data is. Not built yet: a few days' work, waiting on the owner's priority call (decisions A-PARITYMISC-1).
StoreKit's subscription-status view, driven by the App Store. Absent off Apple platforms, and an app run from a terminal is not sold through the App Store.

macOS window and menu-bar chrome: window and menu-bar-extra styles, window placement, which scenes launch or are restored, and the utility window, a panel that floats beside the main window and shows the focused values of whichever main window is key. The terminal emulator owns the one window a TUIkit app draws in, and its scenes are covers stacked over one another (refusal review O9, ruled (b); decisions file Several scenes on one surface (O9)), so nothing floats beside the window in front, and a utility window would have no main window to read while it covered it.

Combine: an ObservableObject injected as an environment object, and a Combine publisher's values. Combine is absent on Linux and Windows. TUIkit's observable path is Observation's: inject with .environment(_:) and read with @Environment(Model.self), the mapping EnvironmentObject's differentShape entry records. A publisher becomes an AsyncSequence consumed in .task(id:).

Haptics need hardware a terminal does not have. The rest of this family once declined with it now ships: Spring and every spring animation, spring loading (SpringLoadingBehavior, a paused drag activating a control), and MeshGradient (drawn per cell, or as a picture where the terminal takes one). The Wave 17 review (P11) puts SensoryFeedback to the owner as O8.

Per-pixel shading: Metal shader functions, colour/layer/distortion effects, blend modes and dynamic range. Every one of them addresses a sample. A terminal cell has one foreground colour, one background colour and a glyph, with no subpixel to shade. The colour effects (brightness, contrast, saturation, grayscale, hue rotation) rewrite cell colours and ship, as View modifiers and as visual effects; `View.opacity` is the one filter that survives, and it survives by resolving at composite time against whatever is behind it (see Documentation/Colour and styling/Opacity as composition.md) rather than by blending pixels. Glass ships as a material's surface with a highlighted rim, no refraction (refusal review O5, Deliberate deviations C11).

No terminal renders HDR: every colour escape a terminal takes is 8-bit sRGB (truecolour SGR, the 256 cube, the 16 slots; OSC 4/10/11 and Ghostty's widest `rgb:`/`rgbi:` specifications are SDR too, Ghostty VT reference adoption study.md), and none reports a display headroom. `Color.ResolvedHDR` and `resolveHDR(in:)` would hand an app linear components and a headroom above 1 that nothing on screen could show, and `exposureAdjust(_:)` would brighten by stops a colour whose top is already the terminal's white — each pretending to a range the medium does not have, which the owner ruled out (decisions A16: "only APIs that fail gracefully; none that pretend"). `Color.headroom(_:)` IS implemented: an SDR display always meets the cap, so the colour comes back as it is. SwiftUI has no query of the shape "is HDR supported" for TUIkit to answer "no" through; `allowedDynamicRange` is a setting, declined with the per-pixel family.

A path's boolean operations and its stroke outline: exact geometric clipping of one outline by another, and offsetting a curve by half a line width, each a computational-geometry library of its own (refusal review W1, 'Not in this cut'). Shapes otherwise ship (Sources/TUIkitFoundation/Shapes): what a stroke or a fill COVERS is drawn exactly, by rasterising the path and the stroke's pieces, but no outline of the result is made as a Path. Absent rather than approximated, so a call fails to compile; a mask-level union or intersection for fills is possible later (decisions file W1).

A shape's LayoutDirectionBehavior — whether it mirrors in a right-to-left layout — waits with the type and `View.layoutDirectionBehavior(_:)` on decisions A3, deferred with right-to-left support (B1): `.mirrors(in: .leftToRight)` really mirrors in SwiftUI (measured), so the property cannot be a constant that compiles and means nothing. Every TUIkit layout is left to right, which is what a shape's `.fixed` would say.

Font.Weight.why: Sources/TUIkitFoundation/Styling/StyleAttributes.swift:24 — the enum is spelled `FontWeight` at the top level, and `Font.Weight` is a typealias to it (Sources/TUIkitFoundation/Styling/Font.swift), so SwiftUI's spelling and every case (`Font.Weight.bold`, `.light`, …) compile verbatim. The audit reads declarations rather than resolving typealiases, so it sees the members only under the top-level name.

GlobalCoordinateSpace.why: `CoordinateSpace.global`, the terminal's top-left cell: the screen, the window's bars included (the space pointer locations are reported in). SwiftUI spells the protocol form as a struct; TUIkit has the struct too, and the tool sees the enum case it resolves to. Exact on the frame that draws it: the scene root finds the reader once it has drawn and corrects it in the same frame (decisions A2).

ImageRenderer.why: Rendering a view off screen into an inspectable result is public: `renderToBuffer(_:context:) -> FrameBuffer`, whose output reads as `FrameBuffer.lines`. There is no image to make: the result is cells.

LocalCoordinateSpace.why: Sources/TUIkitFoundation/Views/GeometryReader.swift:99-100 — `case local`, "Relative to the GeometryReader itself, whose origin is (0, 0)", consumed by `frame(in:)` at :49-58 where it is documented as "always exact". SwiftUI's struct is just the protocol-based spelling of the same case.

ProposedViewSize.why: Sources/TUIkitCore/Rendering/LayoutTypes.swift:16 — `public struct ProposedSize` with `width: Int?` / `height: Int?` and `.unspecified` / `.fixed(_:_:)`. Same role and same nil-means-ideal semantics as `ProposedViewSize`, in cells rather than CGFloat per §2.2. It is what `Layout.

AXChartDescriptorRepresentable.why: Conformance requires AXChartDescriptor from Apple's Accessibility framework, which does not exist on Linux — a hard blocker for a package that must build there (.claude/CLAUDE.md) — and its purpose is VoiceOver's audio graph, for which a pty has no channel.

AccessibilityActionCategory.why: It categorises custom AX actions (.default/.edit) inside the AX actions menu, a VoiceOver UI. TUIkit surfaces extra actions as drawn menus instead (Sources/TUIkitFoundation/Modifiers/ContextMenuPresentation.swift), which need no AX category because they are ordinary visible items.

AccessibilityAdjustmentDirection.why: It exists only as the argument of `accessibilityAdjustableAction`'s callback, which an assistive technology invokes, and a terminal app has none to invoke it. The adjustment a person makes arrives as ordinary key input instead: the arrow keys, through `onKeyPress`.

AccessibilityAttachmentModifier.why: It is the opaque ModifiedContent modifier that carries AX attachments up the view tree (the return type of nearly every accessibility* modifier). With no accessibility attachments to carry — TUIkit has none anywhere in Sources — the type has nothing to represent.

AccessibilityChildBehavior.why: It is the parameter of accessibilityElement(children:) (.combine/.contain/.ignore), describing how children fold into an AX element. TUIkit's render produces a flat cell grid with no element tree, so there are no children to fold.

AccessibilityCustomContentKey.why: It keys reader-only supplementary content used with AXCustomContent.Importance, an Apple-only Accessibility-framework type absent on Linux. Content that is never drawn cannot reach a terminal user.

AccessibilityDirectTouchOptions.why: Its options (requiresActivation, silentOnTouch) configure VoiceOver's direct-touch pass-through on a touch screen. A terminal has no digitizer — input is key bytes and cell-granular SGR mouse reports — so there is nothing to configure.

AccessibilityHeadingLevel.why: h1…h6 exist for rotor navigation over an AX tree. TUIkit draws headings (Sources/TUIkitFoundation/Views/Section.swift:47) but a level number that is never rendered has no consumer in a terminal, where the only 'reader' sees the finished characters.

AccessibilityLabeledPairRole.why: The .label/.content roles only mean something to accessibilityLabeledPair's AX association. The visible pairing a terminal can express already exists as Sources/TUIkitForms/Views/LabeledContent.swift:25.

AccessibilityRotorContent.why: It is the content protocol for rotor entry lists, consumed by VoiceOver's rotor. No assistive technology can attach to a process whose interface is a byte stream on a pty.

AccessibilityRotorContentBuilder.why: A result builder that exists purely to construct AccessibilityRotorContent; with no rotor to build for, the builder has nothing to produce.

AccessibilityRotorEntry.why: An entry in a VoiceOver rotor, optionally scoped to a text range. A terminal exposes no navigable element or text-range model to any assistive technology — the emulator's screen buffer is all that exists outside the process.

AccessibilitySystemRotor.why: Its members (.headings, .links, .tables, .misspelledWords…) name VoiceOver's built-in rotors. TUIkit renders links, tables and headings as characters; there is no rotor UI in a terminal to enumerate them into.

AccessibilityTechnologies.why: An option set of .voiceOver and .switchControl used to ask which assistive technology is active. Neither can attach to a TUIkit process: they inspect a GUI app's AX tree, and a TUIkit app has no window — the terminal emulator owns the only inspectable surface.

AccessibilityTextContentType.why: Its cases (.sourceCode, .console, .spreadsheet…) tune a reader's pronunciation and navigation. The classification is never rendered, and nothing in a terminal reads app-side metadata.

AccessibilityTraits.why: The trait option set (isButton, isSelected, isHeader, allowsDirectInteraction, causesPageTurn…) is AX-tree metadata. TUIkit publishes no AX tree; a terminal app conveys role only by what it draws (button caps, selection highlight, Section headers).

AccessibilityZoomGestureAction.why: It describes a VoiceOver pinch/zoom gesture (direction, location, point). SGR mouse reporting has no pinch and no sub-cell location, and there is no assistive technology to originate the gesture. TUIkit's real zoom is `.imageZoom(_:)` in Sources/TUIkitBitmaps/Views/Image+RenderingOptionModifiers.swift.

AssistiveAccess.why: A Scene that supplies an alternate interface for iOS's Assistive Access mode. A terminal app has no iOS lifecycle and no system mode to supply one for.

BlendMode.why: There is no blend function for it to name. A composite copies each cell over what it covers; the one blend TUIkit performs, `opacity`, resolves at the composite against whatever is behind (Documentation/Colour and styling/Opacity as composition.md). The modes multiply, screen and so on per pixel sample, which a cell does not have: see the per-pixel shading family.

CGPoint.AnimatableData.why: SwiftUI conforms CGPoint/CGSize/CGRect to its Animatable; TUIkit cannot conform them to its own. On Apple platforms SwiftUICore's extension of these CoreGraphics types is visible to any module that imports Foundation (a cross-import overlay), and its `AnimatableData` typealias is found before any witness TUIkit could supply, so the conformance fails to compile there (verified 2026-10-03). TUIkit's geometry is whole cells: `CellSize` and `CellRect` are Animatable (Sources/TUIkitFoundation/Rendering/AnimatableGeometry.swift). `CGFloat` IS conformed: Sources/TUIkitCore/Animation/VectorArithmetic.swift.

CGPoint.applying(_:).why: Applies a ProjectionTransform, a 3-D perspective matrix (declined under its own entry): a cell grid has no projection to apply a point through.

CGRect.AnimatableData.why: SwiftUI conforms CGPoint/CGSize/CGRect to its Animatable; TUIkit cannot conform them to its own. On Apple platforms SwiftUICore's extension of these CoreGraphics types is visible to any module that imports Foundation (a cross-import overlay), and its `AnimatableData` typealias is found before any witness TUIkit could supply, so the conformance fails to compile there (verified 2026-10-03). TUIkit's geometry is whole cells: `CellSize` and `CellRect` are Animatable (Sources/TUIkitFoundation/Rendering/AnimatableGeometry.swift). `CGFloat` IS conformed: Sources/TUIkitCore/Animation/VectorArithmetic.swift.

CGSize.AnimatableData.why: SwiftUI conforms CGPoint/CGSize/CGRect to its Animatable; TUIkit cannot conform them to its own. On Apple platforms SwiftUICore's extension of these CoreGraphics types is visible to any module that imports Foundation (a cross-import overlay), and its `AnimatableData` typealias is found before any witness TUIkit could supply, so the conformance fails to compile there (verified 2026-10-03). TUIkit's geometry is whole cells: `CellSize` and `CellRect` are Animatable (Sources/TUIkitFoundation/Rendering/AnimatableGeometry.swift). `CGFloat` IS conformed: Sources/TUIkitCore/Animation/VectorArithmetic.swift.

Color.Representation.why: The type of Color's transferRepresentation; see that entry.

Color.transferRepresentation.why: Color's Transferable conformance. CoreTransferable is Apple-only, and the terminal's clipboard holds text: TUIkit's copyable/draggable payloads need no Transferable conformance, so there is no representation for a colour to declare (as for Image.transferRepresentation).

ColorMatrix.why: It exists only as the payload of `GraphicsContext.Filter.colorMatrix`, applied per pixel, and with no `GraphicsContext` there is nothing to apply it. A channel transform of a cell's foreground and background is the colour-effect modifiers' ground (`ColorEffectModifiers.swift`).

ColorRenderingMode.why: It selects the colour space a Canvas or an ImageRenderer composites in, linear or non-linear sRGB. TUIkit has neither, and its one blend, `opacity`, is done in encoded sRGB, so the mode would have nothing to select. If `drawingGroup(opaque:colorMode:)` ships (decisions A27), the type comes with it.

ContentShapeKinds.accessibility.why: The accessibility frame and path of a view's accessibility element, for VoiceOver's focus ring and ordering. A screen reader reads a terminal from the text on screen; TUIkit publishes no accessibility elements with frames for a shape to replace. Omitted so the kind fails to compile rather than shape nothing (refusal review P3); ContentShapeKinds ships `.interaction` and `.dragPreview`.

ContentShapeKinds.focusEffect.why: The shape of the focus ring macOS draws round a focused view. TUIkit draws no focus ring a shape could give its outline: focus is shown by the control's own drawing breathing (focus-selection colour rules). Omitted so the kind fails to compile rather than shape nothing (refusal review P3); ContentShapeKinds ships `.interaction` and `.dragPreview`.

ControlSize.init(_:).why: Converts from AppKit's NSControl.ControlSize. TUIkit links no AppKit, as it must build on Linux; the five sizes are TUIkit's own enum's cases.

EdgeInsets.init(_:).why: Converts from AppKit/UIKit's NSDirectionalEdgeInsets, whose values are points. TUIkit insets count cells, so the conversion would have to invent a point-to-cell scale; and TUIkit links no AppKit, as it must build on Linux.

EdgeInsets.inset(by:edges:).why: Grows insets by a RectangleCornerInsets, the per-corner radii of a rounded rectangle (declined under its own entry). Cell geometry has no corner radii to add.

EnvironmentValues.allowsTightening.why: The environment half of allowsTightening(_:); absent for the same reason — a cell grid has no inter-character spacing to tighten.

EnvironmentValues.minimumScaleFactor.why: The environment half of minimumScaleFactor(_:); absent for the same reason — glyph size belongs to the terminal emulator, not to the app.

Font.Design.rounded.why: A rounded face. The terminal draws every cell in the one face its user configured, and no escape sequence asks for another. Font.Design ships .default and .monospaced, the two that describe the terminal's face (Documentation/SwiftUI parity/Refusals re-examined, wave 17 (2026-10-03).md P1).

Font.Design.serif.why: A serif face. The terminal draws every cell in the one face its user configured, and no escape sequence asks for another; macOS's serif also widens text (31 → 34 pt, measured), which a cell cannot. Font.Design ships .default and .monospaced, the two that describe the terminal's face (Documentation/SwiftUI parity/Refusals re-examined, wave 17 (2026-10-03).md P1).

Font.Leading.why: Leading is the space between baselines, measured in fractions of a point. A terminal's baselines are one cell apart, always. The nearest expressible thing is a WHOLE blank row between lines, which TUIkit spells `View.lineSpacing(_:)` (Sources/TUIkitFoundation/Environment/LineSpacing.swift) — a different unit and a different meaning, so it is not this API under another name.

Font.leading(_:).why: Leading is fractional-point spacing between baselines; a terminal's baselines are exactly one cell apart. The nearest expressible thing is a WHOLE blank row between wrapped lines — `View.lineSpacing(_:)` (Sources/TUIkitFoundation/Environment/LineSpacing.swift) — a different unit and a different granularity, so it is not this API renamed. See also the `Font.Leading` entry.

Font.Resolved.ctFont.why: A CoreText font, absent on Linux and Windows, and a terminal draws in the one face the user configured: there is no font object to hand out. Font.Resolved ships the flags a cell can vary (refusal review P2).

Font.Resolved.leading.why: Line spacing in points; a terminal's rows are fixed, and TUIkit's lineSpacing counts whole rows. Omitted so the spelling fails to compile.

Font.Resolved.pointSize.why: A terminal draws every cell at one size, the user's, which the app cannot read in points; omitted so the spelling fails to compile rather than answer a guess.

Font.Resolved.width.why: A font's width axis (condensed, expanded) has no cell equivalent: every glyph advances one cell; omitted as Font.Width is.

GeometryEffect.why: Its one requirement, `effectValue(size:) -> ProjectionTransform`, has no representation here (see ProjectionTransform). TUIkit's geometry customisation point is `Layout`, which places children at whole cells.

GeometryProxy.safeAreaInsets.why: Omitted on purpose, as decisions B6 records: TUIkit's chrome is subtracted from what a view is offered before layout, so no content runs under a bar and the insets would always be zero. The fuller safe area B6 priced, which would make it real, was declined by the owner on 2026-10-12.

HelpLink.init(anchor:).why: Opens an anchor in an Apple Help book through AppKit's NSHelpManager; a terminal has no Help Viewer and Linux no help books. HelpLink(action:) and HelpLink(destination:) ship. See decisions C5.

HelpLink.init(anchor:book:).why: As HelpLink.init(anchor:): an Apple Help book, through AppKit's NSHelpManager, which a terminal app cannot open. See decisions C5.

Image.init(size:label:opaque:colorMode:r.why: An image drawn by a closure into a GraphicsContext. TUIkit's drawing context is a FrameBuffer (see GraphicsContext under differentShape), and code that draws is a view rather than an image: a Renderable, which draws into the cells it is given at every frame instead of into pixels once.

Image.Representation.why: The type of Image's transferRepresentation; see that entry.

Image.Scale.why: The .small/.medium/.large enum for imageScale; the terminal owns the font size and a symbol is one codepoint at that size (Sources/TUIkitStrings/SFSymbols/SFSymbol.swift:62). Documentation/SwiftUI parity/SwiftUI compatibility guide.md:452 records the same constraint for Font generally.

Image.transferRepresentation.why: Image's Transferable conformance. CoreTransferable is Apple-only, and the terminal's clipboard holds text: TUIkit's copyable/draggable payloads need no Transferable conformance, so there is no representation for an image to declare.

ImportFromDevicesCommands.why: Its items import photos and scans from nearby devices (Continuity Camera), which macOS offers to a window it can present a camera picker over. A terminal app has no such service to call, and nothing on the screen for the picker; the menu bar (TUIkitCommands) carries every other standard command set.

LocalizedStringKey.StringInterpolation.a.why: A colour's spoken name comes from Apple's accessibility colour naming, which is private and has no counterpart in the open-source Foundation, and a screen reader reads a terminal only through what is on screen, so a name would have to be drawn. Declined (owner, 2026-10-05; decisions A33, removed when this entry landed): code that uses it does not compile, and the app says what it means in words. Interpolating the colour's description instead would read `Color(…)` aloud, the quiet wrong answer.

OutlineSubgroupChildren.why: The content type of the DisclosureGroup that is SwiftUI's OutlineGroup `Subgroup` parameter, written only inside OutlineGroup's full five-parameter type. TUIkit's OutlineGroup declares the three generic parameters that carry information and drops the two that never vary (`Parent` is always `Leaf`, `Subgroup` always that one DisclosureGroup) — Sources/TUIkitLists/Views/OutlineGroup.swift — so there is no subgroup for this marker to be the content of. Every initializer, for views and for table rows, is SwiftUI's; only spelling the type out by hand differs. Decisions C10.

PointerStyle.image(_:hotSpot:).why: A pointer drawn from a picture, with its hot spot. A terminal takes its pointer's shape by NAME (OSC 22) from the window system's own cursors, and no terminal takes an image for one. The named styles ship where the terminal documents OSC 22 (decisions O12, C-O12-1); this one would have to draw nothing, so it fails to compile.

PreferredColorSchemeKey.why: The preference key behind `View.preferredColorScheme(_:)`, kept out with it (see that entry).

PreviewContext.why: The canvas-supplied context protocol; no canvas can host a terminal view (see PreviewProvider).

PreviewContextKey.why: Key protocol for PreviewContext, which has no host (see PreviewProvider).

PreviewDevice.why: Names a simulator device for the canvas. A TUIkit app's only "device" is the attached terminal, whose size is read live (`\.terminalWidth`/`\.terminalHeight`, Sources/TUIkitFoundation/Environment/ViewEnvironmentKeys.swift:75) and whose glyph repertoire is detected at runtime (TerminalHost)

PreviewModifier.why: Supplies shared context to canvas previews; with no canvas able to host a FrameBuffer-rendering view (see PreviewProvider) there is no preview to modify.

PreviewModifierContent.why: The placeholder content type inside a PreviewModifier; absent for the same canvas-hosting reason.

PreviewPlatform.why: Enumerates iOS/macOS/tvOS/watchOS canvases; TUIkit targets a tty on macOS/Linux (Windows in progress) and has no canvas on any of them.

PreviewProvider.why: Xcode's canvas instantiates a PreviewProvider and hosts the resulting view in a real view hierarchy. A TUIkit view resolves to a text `FrameBuffer`, with no NSView or UIView to host, so the canvas has nothing to show; the headless equivalent is the public `renderOnce(content:)`.

ProjectionTransform.why: A 3×3 matrix over continuous coordinates, produced by GeometryEffect and consumed by `projectionEffect`. TUIkit's geometry is whole cells with no matrix: its only spatial operation is a whole-cell offset. The transforms wait on decisions A27.

SafeAreaRegions.why: An option set over `.container` and `.keyboard`. Neither is a live distinction here: a terminal has no on-screen keyboard, and the container region is the whole grid less the chrome the app declared, subtracted before layout (decisions B6, whose fuller safe area the owner declined on 2026-10-12).

ScrollEdgeEffectStyle.soft.why: A fade of scrolled content seen through a bar. Content never passes under a bar here — bars are subtracted from what the view beside them is offered (decisions B6, whose fuller safe area the owner declined on 2026-10-12) — so there is nothing to see through, and the style is left out so that asking for it fails to compile (refusal review O7, ruled 2026-10-12). `.automatic` and `.hard` describe what is drawn, and ship.

ScrollInputKind.why: Its values are watchOS's — the Digital Crown and the double-tap hand-gesture shortcut — and the macOS SDK defines none, so no macOS source can name one, and View.scrollInputBehavior(_:for:) cannot be called there either. A terminal has neither input. The question macOS code can ask, whether scrolling is allowed at all, is .scrollDisabled (the ScrollInputBehavior entry).

SectionedFetchRequest.why: A Core Data property wrapper, with FetchRequest's family (see that entry): permitted behind #if canImport(CoreData) by decisions A18, not built yet, waiting on the owner's priority call (A-PARITYMISC-1).

SectionedFetchResults.why: The results collection of SectionedFetchRequest: permitted behind #if canImport(CoreData) by decisions A18, not built yet (A-PARITYMISC-1).

SubmitLabel.why:
It names an on-screen keyboard's Return key ('Go', 'Send', 'Search'), and a terminal has no on-screen keyboard. It shipped once as a value stored in the environment that nothing read, which is worse than absence — the call compiled and the developer never learned the affordance does not exist — so it was removed (c5f31f85) and `.submitLabel(.send)` now fails to compile. `.onSubmit`, the behaviour rather than the legend, is fully implemented.

The obvious substitute WAS evaluated and declined 2026-08-17: a status-bar hint ('⏎ Send') while the field holds focus, using the per-focus-section registration StatusBarState already has. Four reasons. (1) It would fight the app for the Return slot: a StatusBarItem's identity IS its shortcut (StatusBarItem.swift — the hover state machine compares it across renders) and `resolvedSectionItems` drops any global item sharing one, so focusing a field would evict an app's own '⏎ select' item and restore it on blur. (2) It could lie: Return only submits when a submit action exists — `combinedSubmitAction` returns nil otherwise, deliberately, so Return falls through to a dialog's default button — so a field with `.submitLabel(.send)` and no `.onSubmit` would advertise 'Send' while Return fired 'Cancel'. Suppressing the hint in that case diverges from SwiftUI, which shows the label regardless. (3) Chrome churn: items joining and leaving on every Tab shift the bar, and at narrow widths can flip it into renderCompact, changing the other items too. (4) `\.statusBar` is Optional, so it would be inert in an app that does not use the bar — the honesty guarantee would not be unconditional.

If revisited, the shape to build is opt-in app/scene-level chrome (a TUI-specific `.submitLabelHint(_:)`, default off) so `.submitLabel` is data the app chooses to render, the Return slot is only contended when asked for, and (2) becomes the app's explicit choice. Trigger to reconsider: a real app wanting it.

SymbolColorRenderingMode.why: gradient vs flat colouring inside one symbol needs sub-glyph colour addressing; the smallest colourable unit is the whole cell (one SGR foreground per run — Sources/TUIkitFoundation/Rendering/ANSIRenderer.swift).

SymbolRenderingMode.why: Names monochrome, hierarchical, palette and multicolour symbol rendering. Only monochrome survives a cell grid: a symbol is one code point drawn in the cell's single foreground colour, so a type distinguishing four modes would have exactly one that changes anything.

SymbolVariableValueMode.why: How a variable-value symbol shows its fraction, by colour or by drawing, both defined over the symbol's layers. TUIkit draws a symbol as one glyph with no layers; the terminal's way of showing a fraction is a glyph ramp, which `ProgressView`, `Gauge` and `Slider` draw.

TabBarMinimizeBehavior.why: Exists only to feed `tabBarMinimizeBehavior(_:)`; the minimized state is a translucent floating pill at a fraction of the bar's height, which a grid of opaque whole-row cells cannot represent.

Text.Layout.why: Lines, runs and run slices with typographic bounds, handed to a `TextRenderer`. TUIkit's laid-out text is a `FrameBuffer` of styled strings with whole-cell widths: no glyphs, no baselines and no fractional positions. It waits with `TextRenderer` on O16 of the refusal review.

Text.LayoutKey.why: The preference key that publishes anchored Text.Layout values to ancestors. Deferred with TextRenderer (owner, 2026-10-12; refusal review O16).

TextAttribute.why: Marker protocol for values attached via Text.customAttribute and read back inside a TextRenderer's run walk. It exists only to feed the custom-rendering pipeline, deferred with TextRenderer (owner, 2026-10-12; refusal review O16).

TextFormattingCommands.why: Its Font and Text submenus format the selection of a rich-text editor. TUIkit's text controls hold plain text until the rich-text TextEditor (decisions A42) lands, so the commands would do nothing (rule 2). Owed with A42: the menu bar (TUIkitCommands) takes it as it takes TextEditingCommands, with the chords open question A42-Q8 decides.

TextInputFormattingControlPlacement.why: Names the OS surfaces (the keyboard's accessory bar, an inspector, a menu) where the system's rich-text formatting controls appear, for `textInputFormattingControlVisibility`. A terminal app has no OS-drawn chrome on its fields: every cell on screen is written by the process itself.

TextProxy.why: The handle a TextRenderer uses to resolve a Text into a Text.Layout. Deferred with TextRenderer (owner, 2026-10-12; refusal review O16).

TextRenderer.why: Protocol whose draw(layout:in:) receives the text's laid-out lines, runs and slices and a GraphicsContext. Glyphs are not the blocker: a Text.Layout maps onto TUIkit's wrapped lines, style runs and grapheme clusters at known cells. The blocker is the GraphicsContext subset it would need (drawing a run with its style, opacity and a whole-cell translation), and typographic bounds, which have no honest value here. Deferred by the owner on 2026-10-12 (refusal review O16).

ToolbarTitleDisplayMode.why: Exists only to feed `toolbarTitleDisplayMode(_:)`; a cell grid has a single glyph size (TUIkit has no Font type), so `.large`/`.inline`/`.inlineLarge` collapse to one representation.

View.allowsTightening(_:).why: It asks the type setter to reduce inter-character spacing so a line fits without truncating. A TUIkit app emits characters and the emulator advances a whole cell per column — 1 for most, 2 for East Asian wide and most emoji, 0 for combining marks. There is no sub-cell spacing to reduce. Fitting text into less space is spelled truncationMode(_:), lineLimit(_:) or ViewThatFits here.

View.minimumScaleFactor(_:).why: It permits shrinking the FONT to fit, down to a fraction of the nominal size. A TUIkit app does not own the font: cell size belongs to the emulator, is chosen by the user, and is identical for every glyph on screen. Nothing in the framework can scale one view's text without scaling the whole terminal.

View.pointerVisibility(_:).why: Hiding the pointer over a view. No terminal documents a name that hides it: CSS's `none` is not among the names Ghostty, kitty or foot read, and iTerm2 and xterm take none. Refused unless `pointer_shape_card.py` finds a name that hides the pointer on a host (decisions O12, C-O12-2); `pointerStyle(_:)` ships.

View.preferredColorScheme(_:).why: Kept out on purpose (owner, 2026-10-04: omit for now; decisions A17, removed when this entry landed). A terminal's look is a palette, and the write half of `\.colorScheme` is `.palette(_:)` (SwiftUI compatibility guide.md §2.5). Choosing a light or dark variant would need palettes in pairs, which TUIkit's are not; it becomes possible if light palettes are wanted for their own sake.

View.scrollInputBehavior(_:for:).why: Takes a ScrollInputKind, which has no value on macOS (see that entry), so no macOS source can call it.

View.submitLabel(_:).why:
It names an on-screen keyboard's Return key ('Go', 'Send', 'Search'), and a terminal has no on-screen keyboard. It shipped once as a value stored in the environment that nothing read, which is worse than absence — the call compiled and the developer never learned the affordance does not exist — so it was removed (c5f31f85) and `.submitLabel(.send)` now fails to compile. `.onSubmit`, the behaviour rather than the legend, is fully implemented.

The obvious substitute WAS evaluated and declined 2026-08-17: a status-bar hint ('⏎ Send') while the field holds focus, using the per-focus-section registration StatusBarState already has. Four reasons. (1) It would fight the app for the Return slot: a StatusBarItem's identity IS its shortcut (StatusBarItem.swift — the hover state machine compares it across renders) and `resolvedSectionItems` drops any global item sharing one, so focusing a field would evict an app's own '⏎ select' item and restore it on blur. (2) It could lie: Return only submits when a submit action exists — `combinedSubmitAction` returns nil otherwise, deliberately, so Return falls through to a dialog's default button — so a field with `.submitLabel(.send)` and no `.onSubmit` would advertise 'Send' while Return fired 'Cancel'. Suppressing the hint in that case diverges from SwiftUI, which shows the label regardless. (3) Chrome churn: items joining and leaving on every Tab shift the bar, and at narrow widths can flip it into renderCompact, changing the other items too. (4) `\.statusBar` is Optional, so it would be inert in an app that does not use the bar — the honesty guarantee would not be unconditional.

If revisited, the shape to build is opt-in app/scene-level chrome (a TUI-specific `.submitLabelHint(_:)`, default off) so `.submitLabel` is data the app chooses to render, the Return slot is only contended when asked for, and (2) becomes the app's explicit choice. Trigger to reconsider: a real app wanting it.

View.toolbarColorScheme(_:for:).why: Follows `View.preferredColorScheme(_:)` (decisions A17, owner 2026-10-04: omit for now; the A28 design study §3.3 sends this here): a bar's look is the palette's, and `.toolbarBackground(_:for:)` states a bar's fill; choosing a light or dark variant for one bar would need palettes in pairs, which TUIkit's are not (decisions TOOLBARS, C-TOOLBARS-1).

View.toolbarTitleDisplayMode(_:).why: Refused with `ToolbarTitleDisplayMode` (refusal review O8, owner 2026-10-12: omit the APIs that are inert on macOS too, so they fail to compile, as `submitLabel` does): macOS ignores it, and a terminal's one-row title has no large or inline form either (decisions TOOLBARS, C-TOOLBARS-2).

WiggleSymbolEffect.custom(angle:).why: A wiggle is one of the symbol effects TUIkit does not draw (decisions A35: a symbol is one glyph in one cell, which can fade but not move along an angle), so the angle form of it would only add API that changes nothing. `.wiggle` itself compiles, being the Symbols framework's own type, and is documented as not drawn.

WindowManagerRole.why: It tells the macOS window manager how to place/associate a window. A TUIkit app has exactly one surface — the terminal's alternate screen buffer — and no window manager to negotiate with; `WindowGroup` exists purely as the scene-shaped entry point (Sources/TUIkitApp/App/Scene.swift)

WindowToolbarFullScreenVisibility.why: Exists only to feed `windowToolbarFullScreenVisibility(_:)`; TUIkit has no window and no window toolbar — the host terminal owns both, and TUIkit only ever knows a rows×columns grid (Sources/TUIkitApp/App/RenderLoop.swift).

KeyEquivalent.clear.why: The keypad Clear key (U+F739). No terminal encoding TUIkit parses gives it a sequence of its own (it sits in Num Lock's position), so a shortcut or onKeyPress on it could never fire. Reopen if a terminal is found to send it, most likely under the kitty keyboard protocol (decisions A4). See decisions C4.

DebugReplaceableView.why: Xcode's previews machinery: the type Xcode substitutes for a view while it hot-reloads a preview. It exists for the Xcode preview canvas, which never hosts a TUIkit view.

DragSession.ID.matches(_:).why: It compares a drag session with AppKit's NSDraggingSession, an Apple-only class a TUIkit drag never is: a terminal app's drags happen inside it, without AppKit (and on Linux without it at all). DragSession and its ID, phase and items ship as values.

DropSession.ID.matches(_:).why: It compares a drop session with AppKit's NSDraggingInfo, an Apple-only protocol a TUIkit drag never conforms to: a terminal app's drags happen inside it, without AppKit (and on Linux without it at all). DropSession and its ID, phase and local session ship as values.

AccessibilityActionKind.how: KeyboardShortcut.defaultAction / .cancelAction, the context-menu keyboard route, onDelete
AccessibilityActionKind.why: Its cases are the standard actions, and each has a real key binding in TUIkit: `.default` is the default action (Return activates the default button), `.escape` the cancel action, `.showMenu` the context-menu keyboard route, and `.delete` a row's `onDelete`.

AccessibilityFocusState.why: SwiftUI needs a second focus-state wrapper because VoiceOver's cursor moves independently of keyboard focus. A terminal has one focus, which `@FocusState` with `focused(_:)` and `focused(_:equals:)` binds (`Sources/TUIkitFoundation/Focus/FocusState.swift`).

Canvas.why: The immediate-mode drawing surface is a conformance: `Renderable`'s `renderToBuffer(context:) -> FrameBuffer`, with FrameBuffer's public initialisers to build the cells. A SwiftUI-shaped `Canvas` over a `GraphicsContext` waits on shapes (O0 of the refusal review), as the review's D3 note says.

DynamicViewContent.why: `DynamicViewContentActions` (`Sources/TUIkitFoundation/Views/DynamicViewContent.swift`) is the internal seam behind SwiftUI's protocol, whose `onMove` and `onDelete` it mirrors. It behaves the same for ForEach; the cost of its being internal is that a custom row container cannot take part.

EditableCollectionContent.why: The same internal seam, `DynamicViewContentActions` (move, delete and drop-insertion actions an enclosing List discovers), with ForEach conforming. The public surface is ForEach's own `onDelete` and `onMove` rather than a protocol.

EnvironmentObject.why: `@Environment(M.self)` with `.environment(_:)` for an `Observable` object; `Environment` itself is the shared type. A deliberate choice in the compatibility doc's §2.3: Observation only, no `ObservableObject`.

EveryMinuteTimelineSchedule.Entries.next.how: `EveryMinuteTimelineSchedule.Entries` is a typealias for `PeriodicTimelineSchedule.Entries`, whose `next()` it is
EveryMinuteTimelineSchedule.Entries.next.why: The two schedules yield the same kind of sequence, evenly spaced dates, so TUIkit's EveryMinuteTimelineSchedule.Entries is a typealias for PeriodicTimelineSchedule.Entries where SwiftUI nests a type of its own. The member exists; the symbol graph files it under the alias's target, so the tool cannot see it under this path.

FocusedObject.why: SwiftUI's @FocusedObject reads an ObservableObject, the Combine-based family TUIkit does not support (Documentation/SwiftUI parity/SwiftUI compatibility guide.md §2.3). The same reading of an @Observable model is `@FocusedValue(Model.self)` (Sources/TUIkitFoundation/Focus/FocusedValue.swift), which SwiftUI also offers and which tracks the properties the body reads, as the ObservableObject wrapper did through objectWillChange.

ForEach.Body.why: ForEach declares `public var body: Never`, as SwiftUI's non-tab ForEach does. The `Body` typealias is inferred rather than written, so symbolgraph-extract emits it for the SDK's interface and not for TUIkit's source: an extraction artifact, not a gap.

GraphicsContext.why: `FrameBuffer` is the drawing context: `composited(with:at:)` to draw, `replacingLines` to write, `clamped(toWidth:height:)` to clip, and its overlays, hit-test regions and animated cells as the layer, interaction and animation channels. It differs in drawing cells, not paths; a path-drawing context waits on O0 of the refusal review.

List.Body.why: Sources/TUIkitLists/Views/List.swift:96 `public var body: some View`, the same shape as SwiftUI's `typealias Body = some View`. The typealias is inferred in TUIkit's source and written in the SDK interface, so the gap is a symbolgraph artifact.

ObservedObject.how: a plain @Observable reference, or @Bindable for write-through
ObservedObject.why: `@Bindable` (shipped) for write-through, or a plain `@Observable` reference passed in, with Observation doing the invalidation. The compatibility doc's §2.3 maps `@ObservedObject var m: M` to those.

ScrollInputBehavior.why: Sources/TUIkitFoundation/Views/ScrollDisabled.swift:66. SwiftUI's automatic/enabled/disabled triple collapses to the Bool environment value; the non-additive nesting semantics match (ScrollDisabled.swift:60-63).

ScrollView.Body.why: Sources/TUIkitFoundation/Views/ScrollView.swift:118 `public var body: some View`. axes and content are public (:79, :82), so Body is the only listed gap and it is an inferred-typealias extraction artifact.

ScrollViewReader.Body.why: Sources/TUIkitFoundation/Views/ScrollViewReader.swift:83 `public var body: some View`; same inferred-typealias artifact.

Section.Body.why: TUIkit's Section has a real `body: some View` returning `_SectionCore`, per the project's rule that a public control is a View with a real body. SwiftUI's declares `Body = Never` and renders as a primitive, so the differing typealias is a deliberate structural choice.

StateObject.why: Documentation/SwiftUI parity/SwiftUI compatibility guide.md:179 states the mapping explicitly; `State` is a shared type (Sources/TUIkitView/State/State.swift) and binds at render time by the view's own identity.

Text.Body.why: Extraction artifact, not a real gap: TUIkit's Text declares `public var body: Never`, so `Body` is inferred as `Never` exactly as in SwiftUI. An inferred typealias is absent from the symbol graph of source, as `ForEach.Body` is.

View.fixedSize().how: View.fixedSize(horizontal:vertical:) — both parameters default to true
View.fixedSize().why: SwiftUI declares two overloads; TUIkit's single one has defaults, so `.fixedSize()` compiles and means the same thing (verified by a `swiftc -typecheck` probe against the built module, not by reading). Adding a no-argument overload would be a second spelling of one idea — what the consolidate-before-adding rule exists to prevent — and the extractor cannot see that a defaulted parameter list already covers the shorter call, so it reports the shape difference as a gap.

View.focusedObject(_:).why: Publishes an ObservableObject (§2.3: no Combine-based family). `.focusedValue(_ object:)` publishes an @Observable object under its type, read back with `@FocusedValue(Model.self)` (Sources/TUIkitFoundation/Modifiers/FocusedValueModifier.swift).

View.focusedSceneObject(_:).why: Publishes an ObservableObject for the scene (§2.3: no Combine-based family). `.focusedSceneValue(_ object:)` publishes an @Observable object under its type, seen wherever the focus is (Sources/TUIkitFoundation/Modifiers/FocusedValueModifier.swift).
